title: Storage models and compression
lead: OLTP/OLAP workloads, row and column storage, PAX, Parquet and lossless encoding.

sections.title: Workloads and physical storage models
sections.html:
Workload determines the storage objective

OLTP has many short concurrent reads/writes over a small entity: the source retrieves a page revision, updates useracct.lastLogin/hostname and inserts a revision. OLAP scans many records to aggregate, exemplified by counting lastLogin values per month for government hostnames. HTAP applies analytics to live operational data without first moving it into another system.

The logical relation remains the same under all layouts. Physical storage decides whether the bytes needed by an operation are adjacent, how many irrelevant bytes must be read and how costly it is to reconstruct or update a tuple. Row, column and PAX layouts answer those questions differently.

PDF pp. 1–6

sections.title: Row storage and column storage
sections.html:
Row-store access paths

The source useracct row places userID,userName,userPass,hostname,lastLogin together in a slotted page, addressed by page/slot RID. An indexed point lookup can retrieve the whole needed row from one data-page location.

For the monthly hostname-based aggregate, however, reading each row also transfers userName/userPass and other unused fields. This wastes I/O and cache capacity. Mixed value domains on one page can also compress poorly. Row storage suits whole-entity operations and straightforward inserts, but is less suited to wide scans over few attributes.

PDF pp. 7–11

Column arrays and tuple reconstruction

A column store groups values of one attribute, often in fixed-width arrays with separate NULL metadata. Corresponding positions identify the same logical tuple across arrays. Dictionary codes can turn variable strings into fixed-size entries.

The aggregate can first inspect hostname and then relevant lastLogin values without reading every user field. Consecutive same-type values improve cache use, vectorised processing and compression. Reading one complete tuple instead gathers several columns; insertion and deletion must preserve positional correspondence or use suitable indirection.

PDF pp. 12–16

sections.title: Hybrid storage and Parquet
sections.html:
PAX row groups

PAX first partitions rows horizontally into groups, then stores each group’s attributes in separate column regions. The source groups rows 0–2 and 3–5: the first A chunk contains a0,a1,a2, while its B/C chunks contain the corresponding b/c values.

A directory records group offsets; each group has local metadata. Grouping bounds the distance between related attributes while retaining column locality inside a group. A footer is convenient for an immutable file because group positions become known as writing proceeds.

PDF pp. 17–18

Parquet hierarchy, metadata and skipping

Parquet organises a file into row groups, column chunks and encoded pages. The source illustrates roughly 128 MB row groups and 1 MB pages as configuration examples. A page can carry min/max/count statistics and repetition/definition levels for nested values; the footer records schema and offsets.

Reading selected chunks supplies projection; statistics can reject a page whose range cannot satisfy the predicate. Repetition/definition levels describe nested structure and missingness separately from encoded primitive values. Row groups provide scheduling units for parallel readers. Schema evolution and skipping depend on compatible readers and metadata, not on arbitrary edits to already-written bytes.

PDF pp. 19–20

sections.title: Lossless compression techniques
sections.html:
Lossless, block and value-aware compression

Compression trades CPU work against storage/transfer volume. The DBMS must restore exact values. General block codecs such as Zstd see byte sequences and usually decompress a block before value access; value-aware encodings exploit column structure.

The source RLE example stores 2,2,2,3,4,4,4,4,4 as (2,3),(3,1),(4,5). Delta stores 2,3,4,5 as first=2 plus differences 1,1,1, which RLE can further compress. Bit packing uses ceil(log₂(max+1)) bits for nonnegative bounded values. Direct operations on compressed runs or dictionary codes can avoid fully decoding some queries.

PDF pp. 21–23

Parquet delta example: all encoding steps

values: 100, 101, 101, 102, 101, 101, 102, 101, 99, 100, 105, 107, 114, 116, 119, 120, 121
reference: 100
block 1 deltas: 1,0,1,-1,0,1,-1,-2
block 1 min: -2; residuals: 3,2,3,1,2,3,1,0
block 2 deltas: 1,5,2,7,2,3,1,1
block 2 min: 1; residuals: 0,4,1,6,1,2,0,0

Subtract each block’s minimum delta, making residuals nonnegative. Block 1 needs 2 bits per residual (16 bits=2 bytes); block 2 needs 3 (24 bits=3 bytes). Decode by adding the saved minimum to each residual and prefix-summing from the preceding value. The source’s illustrative byte ledger is 8+8+1+2+8+1+3=31, versus 17·8=136 raw bytes. It includes the reference, minimum deltas and widths; it is not the full Parquet wire-format overhead.

PDF pp. 24–26

Dictionary codes and layout choice

The city sequence New York,London,Paris,New York,Tokyo,London becomes 1,2,3,1,4,2 with dictionary 1↔New York, 2↔London, 3↔Paris, 4↔Tokyo. Decoding uses the reverse mapping from code to original city. Total space includes both codes and dictionary, not codes alone. Equality can compare common dictionary codes; numerical code order only represents string order if the dictionary was constructed that way.

Row storage favours whole-row transactional access; column/PAX storage favours scans over selected attributes and compression. Neither layout nor codec is universally best: workload, repetition, ordering and update frequency determine the trade-off.

PDF pp. 27–28

quiz.question: What is the minimum number of bits per unsigned value needed to encode residual=[2,0,3,0]?
quiz.explanation: Two unsigned bits have four patterns, 00,01,10,11, representing 0 through 3. The residual maximum is 3, so two bits suffice; one bit would represent only 0 and 1. This counts residual payload, not the first value, minimum delta or format metadata.
